chapters.title: Chapter 41 — The Sponge on the Desk

spans.text: Marina counted nine mourners who still spoke Alexandrian Greek and seventeen who did not. The funeral was small. Her grandmother had wanted it small, and the people who came spoke either the Alexandrian Eudoxia had carried for sixty-five years in Athens or the Athenian her daughter had refused to inherit and refused to replace. Anastasia received condolences without correcting anyone's Greek. Marina, who had spent the morning cataloguing the mourners by their accents because it was the only thing she could think to do, stood a half step behind her mother and held her gloves.

The cemetery was on the south slope of the city. The Greek-Egyptian section was a small plot at the back, where the cypresses thinned and the city spread out toward Piraeus in the afternoon light. Eudoxia had picked the plot twenty years ago, paid for it in francs converted on a holiday, and told no one until the paperwork had to be witnessed. That was Eudoxia. Marina had organized the witnesses herself. She had been twenty-four, a graduate student, and her grandmother had said this is the kind of thing I prefer to do while I can still sign my own name.

The priest read in Greek with a slight Cypriot inflection. Eudoxia had liked him because he did not pretend to be Alexandrian. She had wanted the prayers and not the speeches, and the family had honored it. Marina was grateful. She would not have known what to say. She had spent a career writing about the women her grandmother had been one of, and had not known how to be in a room of them as a granddaughter.

The woman who took Anastasia's hand was perhaps eighty. She wore a small dark hat with a veil and a thin gold cross. She did not introduce herself. She moved past Anastasia and stopped in front of Marina and looked at her for long enough that Marina noticed Anastasia notice. The woman's hands were dry and careful when she took Marina's. She held them.
I knew your grandmother in Alexandria,
the woman said.
I am Lysandra Kallistos.
Thank you for coming,
spans.speaker: Marina

spans.text: Marina said.
Lysandra did not release her hands.
There are some things she did not finish,
spans.speaker: Lysandra

spans.text: she said.
Pragmata pou meinan anoichta. You will know what to do.
spans.speaker: Lysandra

spans.text: The Alexandrian Greek was perfect. The phrase was Eudoxia's phrase. Marina had heard her grandmother use it about a half-translated letter, about a sweater she had not finished, about a question Marina had asked her once at seventeen that Eudoxia had refused to answer that day and had never returned to. Things left open.
I do not know what you mean,
she said.
No,
spans.speaker: Lysandra

spans.text: Lysandra said.
Not today.
spans.speaker: Lysandra

spans.text: She let go and moved on to embrace an elderly man with a beard, one of the nine, and Marina felt a small precise dislocation at the edge of her attention. A phrase her grandmother had used, repeated by a stranger who had known her grandmother in a different accent than the one Eudoxia had used at the end. She would write it down later. She wrote everything down.

When the line ended, Anastasia took two steps back from the grave and looked at it for a long moment. Then she turned to Marina and said in French, c'est fini, allons-nous-en, and Marina took her mother's elbow and they walked together toward the cars.

The reception was held at a small hall in Nea Smyrni that the Returnees Association used for funerals and christenings and the occasional public lecture, of which Marina had once given two. Coffee, water, a tray of small pastries. Eudoxia had said for years that she did not want anyone to fuss. The neighbors had brought trays regardless.

Marina made a slow circuit of the room with a coffee in her hand, because it was the only thing she could do that would not look like nothing. She listened to two old women argue gently about the year of the Suez crisis. She listened to the head of the Association deliver a well-meant remark about Eudoxia's quiet generosity that Marina knew, by trade, had been written from notes and was wrong on at least one date. She did not correct him.
Lysandra Kallistos came across the room toward her. The elderly sat. The younger stood. Lysandra was old enough to sit. She did not.
You teach at the university,
spans.speaker: Lysandra

spans.text: she said.
I do. The bureaucratic record as a source of social history. I have a graduate seminar on refugee identification documents.
My granddaughter sends me your articles. I read them. They are careful. You do not make the mistake your generation of scholars makes, of treating the documents as if they wished to be read.
Thank you.
Your grandmother said you would be either a historian or a lawyer.
She did not tell me she had said so.
She would not have,
spans.speaker: Lysandra

spans.text: Lysandra said.
She used to ask me which I thought it should be. I told her she should not have to decide.
spans.speaker: Lysandra

spans.text: Marina, who had been on her own ground for several sentences and had let it carry her, lost the thread for one full beat. Lysandra waited without watching her wait.
It was kind of you to come,
spans.speaker: Marina

spans.text: Marina said, finally.
I will come to your apartment within the week,
spans.speaker: Lysandra

spans.text: Lysandra said.
Your grandmother's. Yours, now. If that is agreeable.
spans.speaker: Lysandra

spans.text: It had not sounded like a courtesy, and Marina did not think it had been one. Lysandra finished her coffee, set the cup on a low table, and moved away, carefully and without hesitation. The body was older than the will. Marina noted this in the part of her mind that noted everything.

By mid-afternoon the room had thinned. Anastasia let her composure down by perhaps a quarter of a turn, refused a ride, and said she wanted to walk. Marina helped her into a coat the day was too warm for and watched her go down the block at the steady measured pace Eudoxia had taught her. Then she took a taxi to her grandmother's building.

The Greek-Egyptian neighborhood Eudoxia had helped settle in the early 1960s was a tight grid of three- and four-story buildings painted in colors chosen by people who had been refused permission to choose them in their previous lives: ochre, rose, and a particular Alexandrian blue Marina had once written a paper trying to source the pigment of. She had grown up walking these streets with Eudoxia, had spent years afterward avoiding them, and had only recently begun to walk them again.

The stairwell smelled of wax and lemon cleaner, as it had since her childhood. One of the upstairs neighbors had done the stairs every Saturday for forty years and had not stopped now that the woman she had done them for was gone. From the third-floor landing Marina could see Eudoxia's clothesline in the courtyard, two pegs still on it.

The apartment was as Anastasia had left it two days ago. The bed stripped and the linens folded. The blinds open. The objects on the mantel where they had always been. Marina set her bag down by the door and crossed to the desk where Eudoxia had done her correspondence, and opened the top drawer.

Bank statements. A water bill. The Association newsletter. A letter from a cousin in Toronto, already answered; the reply, in Eudoxia's careful French, was folded inside the cousin's envelope, ready to be sent. Marina set it aside to post tomorrow.
Under the stack was a brown paper packet bound with hard wax. Her name was on it in Eudoxia's handwriting. There were no instructions.

She turned it once in the light from the window. The wax bore no signet, only the ridged imprint of a thumb. She caught herself reading the object the way she would read a deposit at the archive, and did not stop herself, because the reading was the only steadiness she had in the room. A signet proves who closed a thing. A thumb in wax proves only that it has not been opened since. Eudoxia had sealed this so that Marina would know no one else had read it.

She sat down in her grandmother's chair. It had been built for a smaller woman and was a quarter inch too low for her, as it always had been. She had sat in it as a child at this same hour, the hour her grandmother had called the good light, while Eudoxia answered the Toronto cousin in French, and she had been given a sheet of the same paper and a pencil and told to make her own letter. She had, at six and at eight, in a hand Eudoxia corrected without unkindness. She had grown past the chair before she understood that it was her grandmother's measure she was growing past.

She thought about Lysandra at the graveside. The perfect Alexandrian Greek, the dry hands, the promise to come within the week, which had not sounded like a courtesy. She set the thought beside the packet. It was not a day for acting. It was a day for noticing, and she had noticed.

She found she was doing the thing she did at the archive when a document resisted her: waiting until the object told her how it wished to be read, rather than imposing a reading on it. She had taught that to graduate students for years. She had not expected to practice it at her grandmother's desk on the afternoon of the funeral.

Outside, the Nea Smyrni street did what it did in the late afternoon: the shops reopening after the long midday close, a child called in from a balcony in Greek and answering in the same. Marina had grown up to these sounds, with this woman, in this chair. She had spent a decade explaining communities like this one to people who had never lived in one, and she had been good at it. She sat now in the center of one with a sealed packet under her hands and understood that she had explained the wrong thing for ten years. She had explained how such communities preserved themselves. She had never explained what it cost the people inside them to keep what they kept.

She read her own name on the packet, in the upright disciplined letters Eudoxia used for anything she meant to last, and understood that this was the last thing her grandmother would ever write to her. Once she broke the seal there would be nothing left unopened between them.

She had been taught by her mother that closed doors were not to be opened, and by her grandmother that some doors were closed for reasons that outlived the person who closed them. She was the daughter of one woman and the granddaughter of the other, and she did not yet know which of them she was going to be about this.

The light left the desk. The packet became a pale shape in the dark with her name on it. Marina went to the guest bedroom she had slept in as a child and lay down in her clothes, and left it sealed until morning.
She opened it the next morning.

She did it at the desk, with the lamp on and the curtains half-drawn against the early sun. She held the wax under the lamp for the length of one careful breath, looking at the thumbprint, the small narrow ridges she had watched press onto her own forehead at seven and at twelve and at thirty-one. Then she broke it.
Inside was a single leather-bound notebook, octavo, the leather dark and waxed and not quite uniformly colored. No title. No name. Roughly a hundred and twenty leaves.

The first page was headed in a confident nineteenth-century Greek hand: ETOS 1922, SPONGIARI, KALYMNOS. Year 1922, sponges, Kalymnos. Below the heading ran hand-ruled columns in pencil faded toward sepia. Date. Grade. Count. Weight. Price per piece. Total. Marina recognized the format at once. It was the standard accounting of a sponge merchant of the period; she had seen it in two museum collections and cited one of them in her dissertation a decade ago.

The entries ran from the spring of 1922 to the autumn of 1947, in the same disciplined hand. The grades were the Kalymnos market grades of the day: finestra, melati, kavadiera, agathia, fina. The prices moved as history said they should, falling with the crash of 1929, recovering partway in the thirties, climbing sharply in the early forties when the German occupation closed the European markets and the surviving merchants raised prices for what little trade remained.
Everything was as it should be. In a different week, the cleanness of the provenance alone would have been a small academic event.
At the seventeenth page she stopped. Then she went back to the first page and started again, with a pencil and a notepad beside her.
She worked for two hours.

The columns did not balance, and they did not balance in a particular way. The arithmetic was correct; she checked it twice. Grade and count and weight had each been entered honestly, and their products should have summed to the totals at the bottom of each page, and almost always did. But on certain pages the totals ran higher by small precise amounts that no combination of entries on the page could produce. Too small to be embezzlement. Too consistent to be accidents.

She took down the magnifying lens Eudoxia had kept in the desk for reading bank statements and went over the right margin of one of the affected pages. The totals themselves were clean. But beside them, inside the thin pencil border, were tiny pencil marks. A single short stroke on some pages. A pair on others. Three on a few.
There was a pattern. She did not yet know what it was.

By eleven she had a worksheet filling half a page: the date of each affected page, the discrepancy, the number and orientation of the marks. She set down the pencil and rubbed the bridge of her nose. The ledger was not only a merchant's ledger. It was a merchant's ledger that had been put to a second use, by a second hand or by the same hand working in a different capacity. The first use had kept the trade honest. The second had been laid over it.

The phrasing came to her in the precise register of her own academic prose, and she let it. The grief that was supposed to be in the room had not arrived. What had arrived was the work, and the work she could do.

There was a second feature she had missed on the first reading. Perhaps one entry in twenty was not in Greek. It was in English, in a different hand: small, upright, Edwardian, the English of someone educated at a missionary school or in a British colonial office, competent and not native. The English entries recorded the same things as the Greek. They carried the same small marks in the margin.
She listed them in order of appearance. Forty-three, across twenty-five years.
Then she copied out the first letter of each, in sequence.
S A S A N P.

Six letters, and the page held the beginning of what might be words in transliterated Greek, though the transliteration was looser than she was used to and she had to read it as if taking dictation. She read the six aloud, quietly, to find the rhythm. It was the rhythm of something, a saying or a song. The phrase wanted to be longer than six. It did not finish itself into anything she recognized.

She copied the six characters in clean block letters onto a fresh sheet, underlined them, and looked at them for a long time. She put the pencil down, because she knew the difference between work she was about to break through on and work that needed a day. The cadence she was reaching for would arrive when it arrived, and forcing it would only fasten a wrong reading to the right material. She taught a seminar unit on that discipline. She had given it the title the patient reading. She had not expected to practice it on her own family's evidence, the morning after the funeral.

Out of habit she turned to a clean page and sketched the article, the way she did with every document of interest, because sketching the argument let her see a document as an argument and not a curiosity. She had sketched perhaps two hundred articles that way across her career and published thirty-one. The rest had been the sketching itself, which was the use.
The marginalized total. A note on rounding-tolerance discrepancies in a sponge-merchant ledger, Kalymnos, 1922 to 1947.

She got as far as the primary scribe, identifiable across two and a half decades by an idiosyncratic kappa, and the secondary scribe, whose period and training she could estimate and whose identity she could not. Then she stopped, because the next section would need the marks resolved, and the marks had not resolved.

She had a colleague at the university, an economic historian named Aristos, who would have understood the discrepancies within five minutes. She had a friend at the National Library who could have named three other ledgers like it in Greek collections. She had Salma. She called none of them.

There was a thing she could decide and a thing she could not, and she separated them now, because separating them was the only way she knew to stand on a floor that had moved. She could not decide yet what to do with the ledger. She could decide that she would understand it before anyone took it from her. Whatever her grandmother had used it for and sealed it against, Marina would be the one who read it correctly first. She had spent her whole life being the person in the room who understood the document. She would be that person here, with her own name on the packet, or she would be no one in it at all. That much she could promise the empty chair across the desk.
At the bottom of the worksheet, in pencil, out of a professional habit of twenty years, she wrote a note for the file:

Received sealed with the depositor's thumb. No explanatory text. Depositor's intent regarding publication unstated. Any use of this material is a posthumous responsibility of the inheritor. Decision deferred.
She read it back. The depositor was Eudoxia. The inheritor was Marina. For the first time in her career, the deferral was not procedural.

She thought of her grandmother in this same chair. Marina had been shown a great deal of Eudoxia's work across her life: the rent paid in cash on the first of the month, the coffee made for the visitor, the careful French reply to the Toronto cousin written within four days of the letter. She had inherited the rhythm of those tasks. She had never once been shown this one.
She washed her face at the kitchen sink. The water was cold. The small linen towel beside the sink still smelled, faintly, of the soap her grandmother had used.
She was drying her hands when the phone in the front room rang.
It rang once and stopped. She crossed the room and picked up the receiver anyway. The display showed an unknown number. The line gave her nothing but a dial tone.

Nobody called this number now. The people who had known Eudoxia knew she was dead; most of them had stood at the cemetery the day before. Marina set the receiver back in its cradle and stood with her hand on the small table, looking across the room at the ledger open on the desk and the six letters she could not finish, written out in clean block capitals beside it.
Then she went back to the desk and sat down, and for the rest of the afternoon she did not leave the chair.
When the light was gone she switched on the lamp and let it fall on the closed ledger. She left it there, with the worksheets squared beside it, for the morning.
Lysandra came on the morning of the third day.

Marina had slept badly for two of the three nights. She had spent the second day at the small Returnees Association office, helping a volunteer sort Eudoxia's bequest: forty-three folders of correspondence, photographs, and meeting minutes from 1962 to 2019, most of it her grandmother's own work as the association's archivist before her health moved her to a smaller role. The volunteer was an elderly man named Constantine, who had come from Cairo in 1962 at thirty-five and kept the association's books for forty years afterward. At the door, with four boxes waiting for a taxi, he said he would call her if he needed help reading her grandmother's notes, because Eudoxia had used a French shorthand he did not always follow. Marina said of course. She did not say that she had not known her grandmother used French shorthand.

He also handed her a folder from Eudoxia's desk at the office, one that had not been labeled for transfer. It held two letters from the cousin in Toronto, a clipped French article about the Greek-Egyptian community in Montreal, and a list of names in Eudoxia's hand that Marina took thirty minutes to recognize as the guests at her own wedding, to a man she had divorced six years ago. She set the folder aside. She did not open the ledger again.
On the third morning she was at the desk with coffee at her elbow and the ledger closed on the desk pad when the doorbell rang at twenty past nine.

Lysandra was on the landing in the same dark coat she had worn at the funeral, with a small handbag and the thin gold cross. She gave Marina her coat in the entryway and walked into the front room without being shown the way. At the threshold she stopped and looked at the room for a long moment. Then she crossed to the small armchair Eudoxia had liked and sat, and Marina saw that Lysandra's body remembered the chair. She did not have to settle the cushion against her shoulders.
You have not been here often since she died,
spans.speaker: Lysandra

spans.text: Lysandra said.
I have been here. Not often, no.
I will have coffee if it is no trouble.

Marina made it in Eudoxia's small briki, two spoons, medium sweet, the way Eudoxia had made it for visitors, and brought it out with a plate of paximadi. Lysandra took her cup in both hands. She did not touch the paximadi.

She looked around the room while she drank: the mantel, the shelf above the desk where two of Marina's own books stood among older volumes in Greek and French and one in Arabic Marina had never been able to read, the window onto the courtyard. She looked at the desk last. She looked at the ledger for the length of a careful breath, said nothing about it, and returned to her cup.
Have you opened the packet,
she said.
Marina had prepared several answers. She used none of them.
I have opened it.
spans.speaker: Marina

spans.text: Have you read it.
Enough to see what kind of document it is. I have not finished it.

Lysandra closed her eyes for a long moment. When she opened them, the look she gave Marina was not the look of an elder deciding whether a younger woman could be trusted. It was the look of a person who has already decided and is examining the cost.
There are some people who would like to know what is in that document,
she said.
They will arrive at your door within the week.
Who.
I will not tell you who. They will tell you who they are. They will not be honest about it; you will be honest about reading them.
What do they want.
They want what is in the document. Or what they think is in it. They have not been able to determine that, in their case.

The precision was not stalling. The old woman was choosing how much to say and saying exactly that much, in a cadence Marina had heard at her grandmother's table: Alexandrian, not Athenian, the cadence her mother had refused to inherit and Marina had not known she carried.
You will not tell me what is in it,
spans.speaker: Marina

spans.text: Marina said.
I will not.
It came without softening, with the economy of a woman who had refused this question before and would refuse it again.
You will not tell me what my grandmother used it for.
I will not.
The second refusal had a different texture. Something thinned in it. This one was costing Lysandra a thing the first had not, and her face had not closed. She was waiting.
You will not tell me when she gave it to you to give to me.
Lysandra did not blink.
I will not tell you that either.
spans.speaker: Lysandra

spans.text: Marina understood, without its being said, that Lysandra had never been given the packet. She had come on her own. And she was being asked the questions in the order she had decided, before she walked in the door, that she would refuse them.
In the kitchen the briki ticked once as the metal cooled.
You came to my mother's house,
spans.speaker: Marina

spans.text: Marina said,
and now to my house, and you used her phrase to me, and you knew when she made the packet.
spans.speaker: Marina

spans.text: I knew when she made the packet. Some years ago. She did not tell me how she would arrange to give it to you, or when. She had been deciding, on and off, for ten years. We did not discuss it.
Why did she keep it sealed.
That is the question I came to ask you, Kyria Selene. Whether you have considered what your grandmother's reasons may have been.
She let a moment pass.
And whether those reasons survived her.

Marina had no answer, and could see that an improvised one would not help. She let the silence sit. Her grandmother's silences had always been silences Eudoxia controlled. This one Marina was being permitted to enter, and she entered it carefully.

When Lysandra spoke again it was more quickly. Marina had heard the same change once in a witness she interviewed for her dissertation, an old woman from Constantinople who had spent forty years not telling a story and then told it in three sentences, because the deciding had taken the forty years.
I am sorry to come to you with no comfort.
You owe me no comfort.
That is true. I owe your grandmother. I am paying her back in a way she would have understood.
She leaned forward, the lean of a person preparing to stand who has decided not to stand yet.

There are two things you should know before they arrive. The first is that you will not recognize them when they arrive. The second is that you will recognize them after, and you will be tempted to think that recognition is the one you needed at the door. It is not. It comes after. You will use it for what comes after. Do not use it for the door.
The sentences had the cadence of a thing said before, in this order.
You have given this advice before.
I have. Not in this room.
To whom.
I will not tell you.
She leaned back, and the quickness left her.

I want to ask you one thing more. Do not call the police about whoever arrives. Do not call a lawyer beyond the lawyer you already have. Do not call your mother. Do not call me. Do not call your colleagues at the university or your colleagues at the National Library. There will be a small list of people who can be useful to you. None of them are on this morning's list of the people you might think to call.
Who is on the small list.

The small list is being assembled. You will know one of them within the week, possibly the morning of the arrival itself. You will know a second within the month, possibly sooner. The others will come into view as they come into view. The list is not long. It is sufficient.
You will not tell me whether you are on it.
You will not need to know that. I will come when I am needed. Do not call me before. I will not answer.
I do not have your number.
You will. It will be in the directory at the Returnees Association under my late husband's name. Kallistos was my husband. I have kept his name. He has been dead for thirty-one years.

She stood, more slowly than she had moved at the funeral. In the entryway she let Marina straighten the collar of her coat, which had folded under, and the acceptance was the closest she came all morning to softening.
You will see me again before this is finished,
she said.
I have told you when not to call. I have not told you when I will come. You will not have warning.

At the door she turned. The look was not unkind, and it was not kind either. Marina would later remember it as the look of someone passing a piece of luggage to a stranger at a station, in full faith that the stranger had been correctly identified.
Pragmata pou meinan anoichta,
spans.speaker: Lysandra

spans.text: Lysandra said. The consonant of the second word softened, and the second vowel of anoichta lengthened, the way only the Alexandrian women of her generation lengthened it.
Your grandmother said it differently than I say it. You should listen for the difference.
spans.speaker: Lysandra

spans.text: How did she say it.
spans.speaker: Marina

spans.text: That is the listening. I will not do it for you.
spans.speaker: Lysandra

spans.text: Marina did not press. Lysandra gave her the small slow nod she had given the old man in the receiving line, and went down the stairs, uneven and careful and steady, without stopping at the third-floor landing. The street door opened and shut.

Marina sat down in Eudoxia's chair, in front of the ledger, and tried to hear her grandmother saying the phrase. She could. The cadence was Lysandra's, almost. The almost was in the second word. Lysandra softened the consonant fully. Eudoxia had softened it less, by a small precise margin Marina heard only now, the way she had found the second hand in the ledger on the eighth page of her first read-through. Her grandmother had carried the Alexandrian inflection and withheld a fraction of it. Lysandra withheld nothing. The fraction was that of a woman who had been pretending, very slightly, to belong to the city where she had spent the second half of her life.
The phone in the front room rang once and stopped.

It had rung this way before, a single ring from an unknown number, dead before she reached it. This time, when she crossed to the table and lifted the receiver out of an instinct she did not examine, the line was open. There were a few seconds of a street she did not recognize, traffic in a register that was not Athenian. Then a man's voice, low and unhurried, said her name. Kyria Selene. He said nothing after it. The line went dead while she was still deciding whether to answer.

She had not known the voice. She had known the Greek. It was Athenian, and studied, the inflection laid on a fraction too evenly, the way a phrase is even when it has been practiced for a room rather than spoken in one. It was Greek a person had decided to use. Lysandra had said they would arrive within the week, and that Marina would not recognize them at the door. Standing at the small table with the light going down the wall, Marina understood that the door had already begun, and that it had a voice, and that the voice had her name and her number and the patience to use neither.
